relationship: Same-chapter death proposal contrasted with the king's sworn reversal
rationale: Saul speaks of putting David to death, whereas after Jonathan's intervention he swears by the living Lord that David shall not die. These are distinct stated positions within the same episode.

relationship: Same-chapter jonathan and Michal warn David of stated death plans
rationale: Jonathan warns David to hide before Saul's intended killing; Michal later warns that escape that night is necessary before a morning killing. The warnings preserve their different speakers and occasions.

relationship: Same-chapter planned intercession and its reported outcome
rationale: Jonathan proposes speaking to his father about David and reporting back; the following account gives his defense, Saul's oath and Jonathan telling David the words before bringing him back.

relationship: Same-chapter the innocence defense developed through a particular deliverance
rationale: Jonathan says David has not sinned against Saul and has done good; his next statement cites the foreigner's defeat and calls killing David innocent blood without cause, specifying his defense rather than independently deciding the case.

relationship: Jonathan's recollection of the foreigner's defeat
rationale: Jonathan recalls David striking the foreigner and attributes the deliverance to the Lord; the earlier account narrates the stone strike and subsequent sword killing. The reported recollection and earlier narrated actions retain their different detail.

relationship: Same-chapter the sworn promise contrasts with the earlier death proposal
rationale: Saul's oath that David shall not die answers the episode's opening discussion of putting him to death; Jonathan's intervening defense remains part of the actual context.

relationship: Same-chapter report and return carry out Jonathan's announced mediation
rationale: Jonathan earlier promises to speak to Saul and report what happens; he now tells David all the words and brings him before Saul again, identifying the specific outcome of that mediation.

relationship: Repeated foreigner-defeat language in distinct David campaigns
rationale: Both accounts describe David fighting the foreigners, their flight before him and a great blow. The later action saves Keilah, whereas this unit reports another war against Saul; the two occasions are not collapsed.

relationship: David's playing during Saul's evil-spirit episodes
rationale: The earlier account has David play the kinyra when an evil spirit comes upon Saul and reports relief; the later scene has an evil spirit of God, Saul sleeping with a spear and David playing, followed in context by an attack rather than an assumed identical outcome.

relationship: Same-chapter the spear and playing scene develops into the attempted killing
rationale: The preceding scene places the spear in Saul's hand while David plays; Saul then tries to drive it into David, strikes the wall instead and David escapes. The earlier sleeping description is preserved.

relationship: Saul's spear used in distinct attempts against David and Jonathan
rationale: Saul tries to drive the spear into David and hits the wall; he later raises the spear against Jonathan to kill him. The accounts name different intended victims and do not report an actual spear wound in either unit.

relationship: A psalm heading explicitly recalls Saul's house-watch death plan
rationale: The narrative has Saul send messengers to watch David's house in order to kill him; the supplied Greek-numbered psalm heading expressly names Saul sending and watching his house to put him to death.

relationship: Same-chapter the night-escape warning followed by the window rescue
rationale: Michal warns that David must save his life that night before a morning killing; she then lowers him through the window, and the account says he fled and was saved.

relationship: Women lower threatened visitors through a window
rationale: Michal lowers David through the window to escape; Joshua reports the woman lowering the men through the window. The comparison concerns that particular rescue action and does not add a rope or identical city circumstances to these supplied units.

relationship: Same-chapter the prepared bed substitutes are later discovered
rationale: Michal places funerary images and a goats' liver on the bed; the messengers later find those same objects there. The supplied objects are preserved rather than changed into hair or another arrangement.

relationship: Same-chapter reported illness followed by the king's bed-transport demand
rationale: The messengers say David is ill; Saul's following demand is to bring him on the bed so that he may kill him. The report of illness is not treated as a narrator's confirmation that David is sick.

relationship: Same-chapter the demand for David on the bed meets the discovered substitutes
rationale: Saul orders David brought on the bed for killing; the following inspection instead finds the funerary images and liver. The connection preserves what the messengers actually find rather than reporting David transported to Saul.

relationship: Same-chapter discovery repeats the deliberately prepared objects
rationale: The messengers find funerary images on the bed with goats' liver at its head, repeating Michal's earlier placement of those particular substitutes.

relationship: Same-chapter saul's escape accusation refers to Michal's narrated rescue
rationale: Saul accuses Michal of sending David away so that he escaped; the earlier account narrates her lowering him through the window and his escape. Her additional claim of a threat remains reported speech, not a separately narrated threat.

relationship: Same-chapter the actual lodging becomes the subject of Saul's report
rationale: David and Samuel stay at Nauath in Ramah after David reports Saul's actions; the next unit tells Saul that David is at that named place.

relationship: Same-chapter the report's location matches the preceding lodging notice
rationale: The report to Saul places David at Nauath in Ramah, where the preceding account has David and Samuel staying; no modern site identification is added.

relationship: Same-chapter god's Spirit brings prophecy to messengers and then Saul
rationale: The Spirit of God comes on Saul's arresting messengers and they prophesy; when Saul goes himself, the Spirit comes upon him too and he goes on prophesying. The participants remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter successive messenger parties repeat the first prophetic outcome
rationale: The second and third groups also prophesy after the first party's Spirit-associated prophecy, forming a stated escalation of Saul's repeated attempts to send messengers for David.

relationship: Same-chapter saul's inquiry receives the location already reported to him
rationale: Saul asks where Samuel and David are and is told Nauath in Ramah; the earlier report had already placed David there. Armathaim and Sephi remain the supplied descriptions of Saul's approach.

relationship: Same-chapter saul shares the prophetic outcome first reported of his messengers
rationale: God's Spirit comes upon Saul as it earlier came upon the messengers, with prophesying in each case. The later unit does not turn Saul into one of the earlier messenger parties.

relationship: The Saul-among-the-prophets proverb recurs
rationale: The naked prophesying episode ends with the saying Is Saul also among the prophets; the earlier account records that same saying becoming a proverb after Kish's son is seen prophesying.

relationship: David's innocence question echoes Jonathan's earlier defense
rationale: David asks what wrong or sin has led Saul to seek his life; Jonathan earlier argued to Saul that David had not sinned and that killing him would shed innocent blood. The question and defense remain their respective speakers' words.

relationship: Same-chapter jonathan's initial confidence and later recognition of the death purpose
rationale: Jonathan initially says Saul would not hide a decision from him; after the spear threat, he expressly knows Saul has determined to kill David. The comparison follows those stated assessments without inventing an unreported prior disclosure.

relationship: The favour David invokes is independently stated in the earlier narrative
rationale: David attributes Saul's concealment to knowledge of Jonathan's favour; the earlier narrator explicitly says Jonathan greatly favours David. Saul's alleged concealment rationale remains David's attribution.

relationship: Same-chapter jonathan's offer receives David's specific hiding request
rationale: Jonathan asks what David desires and what he should do; David responds with the new-moon absence and a request to hide in the plain until evening.

relationship: Same-chapter the planned hiding and new-moon meal are narrated
rationale: David proposes hiding instead of eating with the king at the new moon; the later unit states he hid in the field and that the king came to the table when the month arrived.

relationship: Same-chapter the proposed Bethlehem explanation is delivered to Saul
rationale: David supplies a request-for-leave story about a yearly tribal sacrifice at Bethlehem; Jonathan later delivers the Bethlehem and tribal-sacrifice explanation, adding the quoted brothers' command. Neither statement independently verifies that the sacrifice occurred.

relationship: Same-chapter the proposed test of hostile intent reaches an explicit conclusion
rationale: David says a harsh answer will show evil determined against him; after Saul raises the spear against Jonathan, the narrator says Jonathan knows Saul has determined to kill David.

relationship: Same-chapter the invoked Lord-covenant is recalled in the farewell oath
rationale: David bases his plea for mercy on their covenant of the Lord; the farewell recites their oath in the Lord's name and His permanent witness between them and their seed, without dating the original covenant beyond the supplied statements.

relationship: Same-chapter the promise to report evil and the departure code
rationale: Jonathan promises to report the father's intended evil; the later agreed beyond-you signal means David must go. The unusual and-if-not wording of Jonathan's actual promise is not replaced with a different conditional.

relationship: Same-chapter the question about communication is answered by the shaft signals
rationale: David asks who will tell him about a harsh answer; Jonathan's later plan assigns the little boy's shaft search two distinct messages, one of safety and one of departure.

relationship: Same-chapter the field instruction is followed by David's concealment there
rationale: Jonathan tells David to remain in the field and both go there; later David is expressly hidden in the field while the king's meal begins.

relationship: Same-chapter the communication pledge and accompanying oath
rationale: Jonathan promises to question his father and communicate good concerning David; the adjoining oath speaks of uncovering David's ear and sending him in peace. Its actual bring-the-evils-upon-you clause is preserved rather than silently rewritten.

relationship: Comparable oath invocations asking God or the Lord to act and add
rationale: Jonathan invokes God to do so to Jonathan and more besides; Ruth invokes the Lord to do these things to her and add these things. The formula accompanies different personal undertakings and does not harmonize their additional clauses.

relationship: Same-chapter the personal mercy request extends to the house and name
rationale: The request for mercy while Jonathan lives continues into a plea not to remove mercy from his house or his name from David's house. The preceding may-it-not-be supplies the sense of the sentence continuing through verse16.

relationship: David later asks to show house-mercy for Jonathan's sake
rationale: Jonathan requests enduring mercy for his house; David later asks whether anyone remains of Saul's house so he may show mercy for Jonathan's sake. The connection concerns the explicit mercy motive rather than equating every member of the two houses.

relationship: Same-chapter house-and-name preservation and the enduring oath between seed
rationale: The plea concerning Jonathan's name in David's house belongs to the preceding mercy request; the farewell oath explicitly includes the two men's seed for ever, giving a later statement of the bond's family scope.

relationship: Same-chapter the renewed oath follows the request concerning Jonathan's house
rationale: Jonathan swears again because he loves the soul of the one who loves him, immediately after the mercy and house-name plea. The actual reciprocal-love wording is preserved rather than changed into an ownsoul comparison.

relationship: Same-chapter the predicted seat inspection is expressly narrated
rationale: Jonathan predicts David will be sought when his seat is inspected at the new moon; the meal account explicitly reports David's place being inspected.

relationship: Same-chapter the designated ergab hiding place is the place of emergence
rationale: Jonathan directs David to remain beside the ergab; after the boy enters the city, David rises from the ergab. The untranslated place-object is not independently identified as a particular stone or modern location.

relationship: Same-chapter the planned shaft acts and the later narrated hurl
rationale: Jonathan plans three acts with shafts toward the amattari; the later scene narrates the boy running and Jonathan hurling a shaft past. That singular report is not expanded into independent confirmation of all three planned acts.

relationship: Same-chapter contrasting agreed messages of safety and departure
rationale: The shaft on this side means David may come in peace without danger; the shaft beyond means he must go because the Lord has sent him away. These are the explicitly opposed conditions of the same signal plan.

relationship: Same-chapter the beyond-you warning is actually called out
rationale: The agreed beyond-you shaft message means departure; Jonathan later shouts that exact beyond-you location to the boy. The meaning comes from the earlier stated code rather than the boy's knowledge.

relationship: Same-chapter the Lord's permanent witness is repeated in the farewell
rationale: Jonathan invokes the Lord as witness between himself and David for ever; the farewell repeats the permanent witness formula and expressly includes their seed.

relationship: Same-chapter field hiding and the meal follow David's announced plan
rationale: David is hidden in the field while the king sits to eat as the month arrives, matching the earlier plan to miss the new-moon meal and hide instead.

relationship: Same-chapter the seat inspection answers Jonathan's specific prediction
rationale: The meal scene reports David's place inspected after Jonathan predicted his inspected seat would cause him to be sought. Saul's stated seating and preceding Jonathan are not altered into a different arrangement.

relationship: Same-chapter the first-day purity conjecture gives way to a second-day question
rationale: Saul initially says nothing and conjectures David is unclean; on the next, second day he asks why Jesse's son has missed both meals. The conjecture is not verified as David's actual ritual condition.

relationship: Same-chapter saul's inquiry is the situation anticipated in the proposed explanation
rationale: Saul asks why Jesse's son has not come to the table; David had provided Jonathan a Bethlehem explanation for the event that Saul inquired after him. The actual yesterday-and-today question remains distinct from the plan's general condition.

relationship: Same-chapter jonathan repeats the Bethlehem request-for-leave explanation
rationale: Jonathan tells Saul that David sought leave for Bethlehem, his city, repeating that particular part of David's earlier proposed answer without independently narrating a journey there.

relationship: Same-chapter the reported tribal-sacrifice explanation expands the proposed story
rationale: Jonathan's quotation gives a tribal sacrifice and the brothers' command at the city, corresponding to David's proposed yearly tribal-sacrifice explanation. The additional words remain part of the delivered report rather than independently verified events.

relationship: Same-chapter saul's companion accusation corresponds to David's stated expectation of known favour
rationale: David had said Saul knew Jonathan favoured him; Saul's later rebuke calls Jonathan Jesse's son's companion. The rebuke supplies that stated association without confirming every motive David attributed to his father.

relationship: Opposed accounts of David and Jonathan's prospective kingship
rationale: Saul says Jonathan's kingship cannot be established while David lives; Jonathan later says David will reign and he himself will be second. These are the two speakers' contrasting political prospects, not a claim that every predicted role is fulfilled.

relationship: Jonathan repeats the defense against an unexplained death sentence
rationale: Jonathan asks why David should die and what he has done; he had earlier defended David as having committed no sin and challenged killing him without cause, repeating the particular innocence argument to Saul.

relationship: Same-chapter the death-purpose conclusion follows the proposed harsh-answer test
rationale: After Saul raises the spear against Jonathan, Jonathan knows the evil determined against David is killing; the earlier plan had identified a harsh response as the sign of evil determination.

relationship: Same-chapter father's angry rebuke contrasted with the son's furious withdrawal
rationale: Saul burns with anger against Jonathan; Jonathan later leaves the table in furious anger and does not eat, explicitly crushed over David. The final him in the father's determination is not independently reassigned.

relationship: Same-chapter the boy accompanies the arranged field visit described by the signal plan
rationale: Jonathan comes to the field as arranged with a little boy; the earlier plan had assigned a little boy to find the shaft while Jonathan spoke a coded message. This unit begins the action without asserting that the safety message has been delivered.

relationship: Same-chapter the narrated hurl performs a shaft action in the earlier plan
rationale: Jonathan tells the boy to find the shafts and hurls a shaft past as he runs; the earlier plan specifies shaft acts toward the amattari. No bow or complete three-act sequence is added to this narrated unit.

relationship: Same-chapter the shouted shaft position carries the agreed departure message
rationale: Jonathan says the shaft is beyond the boy, precisely the location the earlier code assigned to David's departure; the boy's physical search and David's understood message remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter the boy gathers the shafts he was told to find
rationale: The boy's hurried gathering follows Jonathan's instruction to run and find the shafts. The supplied shift from a narrated singular shaft to gathered shafts is retained without inventing additional shots.

relationship: Same-chapter the boy's ignorance contrasts with the agreed double message
rationale: Only Jonathan and David know the matter; their earlier plan gives the boy's shaft search a coded safety-or-departure meaning, explaining the stated contrast in knowledge without attributing that knowledge to the boy.

relationship: Same-chapter the attendant's dismissal precedes David's emergence
rationale: Jonathan sends the boy into the city; the next unit expressly begins when the boy has entered and then describes David rising from the ergab for the bowing, kisses and weeping.

relationship: Same-chapter david emerges from the particular designated hiding point
rationale: David rises from the ergab after the boy goes, matching Jonathan's earlier instruction to stay beside the ergab. Neither the place-object nor the great-completion wording is replaced by an unsupplied identification or comparison.

relationship: The enduring Lord-witnessed oath and a later covenant meeting
rationale: The farewell invokes the Lord's permanent witness between the men and their seed; their later meeting again expressly places the two men's covenant before the Lord, without repeating all the earlier oath's wording.

relationship: David's departure follows Jonathan's go-in-peace farewell
rationale: Jonathan tells David to go in peace under their oath; the next chapter states David rose and went away while Jonathan entered the city, preserving the different departures.

relationship: The Nomba priestly visit is later specifically reported
rationale: David arrives at Nomba to Abimelech the priest; Doeg later reports seeing Jesse's son arrive there to Abimelech son of Ahitub, adding the stated patronymic without changing the supplied name.

relationship: The royal-mission claim contrasts with the king's conspiracy accusation
rationale: David tells the priest of a secret royal commission; Saul later calls the priest's bread, sword and inquiry assistance a conspiracy. These opposed reported claims are not merged into an independently verified royal mission.

relationship: Same-chapter the bread request is answered with the available presentation loaves
rationale: David asks for five loaves or whatever is available; Abimelech later gives the loaves of presentation because no other bread is there. The number actually handed over is not independently supplied.

relationship: Holy loaves and the law assigning the bread to Aaron's sons
rationale: The priest distinguishes common from holy loaves and states an abstinence condition; Leviticus assigns the continual bread to Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place. That law does not state the particular reported abstinence condition here.

relationship: Same-chapter the abstinence reply addresses the priest's condition
rationale: David reports abstinence and the young men's purification in reply to the priest's stated woman-abstinence condition. His additional common-road and equipment-sanctification wording is preserved without an independent ritual explanation.

relationship: Jesus explicitly recalls David's use of the presentation bread
rationale: The priest gives David the loaves of presentation; Jesus later recalls David and his companions' hunger and eating the bread of the Presence normally reserved for priests. The earlier unit's handing-over and replacement details remain distinct from Jesus' recalled meal.

relationship: The replaced bread relates to the continual presentation ordinance
rationale: The narrative describes bread removed from before the Lord so that hot bread could be set out; Leviticus commands its continual Sabbath setting and assigns the holy bread to Aaron's sons. The comparison does not add an unreported date for David's visit.

relationship: Doeg's Syrian designation and mule office recur in the report scene
rationale: The earlier visitor is Doeg the Syrian tending Saul's mules; the later speaker is again Doeg the Syrian appointed over those mules, now reporting David's visit. No different ethnic designation is substituted.

relationship: Same-chapter the weapon request receives the specific sword offer
rationale: David asks whether a spear or sword is available and gives royal urgency as his explanation; the priest offers Goliath's sword as the only one there. The royal explanation remains David's speech.

relationship: The offered Goliath sword relates to David's narrated victory
rationale: The priest offers the sword of the foreigner Goliath whom David struck; the battle account describes David taking the sword and beheading the fallen foreigner. The intervening custody of the weapon is not independently narrated.

relationship: Same-chapter the sword handover follows the offer and David's request
rationale: The priest offers the only sword and David says to give it to him; the next unit states that he gave it to him before David's flight to Achish. The pronouns remain in their supplied dialogue context.

relationship: The earlier victory song is repeated at Achish's court
rationale: Achish's servants quote the women's earlier allocation of Saul's thousands and David's tens of thousands. Their additional king-of-the-land label remains their speech rather than an independent coronation notice.

relationship: Same-chapter david's fear follows the specific identifying words at court
rationale: David puts the servants' words in his heart and fears Achish; the preceding words identify him and repeat the victory song. The link concerns the stated verbal occasion of his fear rather than a clinical diagnosis.

relationship: Same-chapter the performed behavior receives Achish's reported fits assessment
rationale: David alters his face, pretends, drums on the doors and has saliva on his beard; Achish then calls him a man subject to fits. The king's assessment is not independently verified as an actual illness.

relationship: Same-chapter achish's assessment responds to the narrated performance
rationale: Achish describes a man subject to fits after David's altered-face, pretended behavior is narrated; the relation preserves reported diagnosis versus performed action and adds no medical mechanism.

relationship: The refusal of house entry is followed by escape to Adullam
rationale: Achish refuses this man entry into a house; the next account has David leave that setting and escape to Adullam's cave. No additional formal expulsion speech is inserted.

relationship: A psalm heading names David's cave flight from Saul
rationale: The narrative places David's escape into Adullam's cave; the psalm heading names his escape from Saul's presence into a cave. The heading does not name the cave, so this connection does not identify which narrative cave episode it represents.

relationship: About four hundred with David at two points in the fugitive account
rationale: About four hundred distressed men gather with David as leader; later about four hundred leave Keilah with him. The actual matching estimates do not independently establish identical rosters or constant strength between the two notices.

relationship: Same-chapter the request for parental shelter is followed by their stay
rationale: David asks Moab's king to let his father and mother stay until he knows what God will do; the next unit says they stayed with the king during David's stronghold days.

relationship: Same-chapter the parents' stay answers David's specific request
rationale: The reported stay with Moab's king follows David's plea for shelter for his father and mother. It does not say that every member of David's household relocated there.

relationship: Gad gives David direction in distinct prophetic settings
rationale: Gad the prophet directs David to leave the stronghold for Judah; the later account calls Gad the prophet and David's seer and sends him with the Lord's message to David. The instructions and circumstances remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter the standing servants are identified as the audience of Saul's appeal
rationale: Saul's servants stand beside the seated spear-holding king; the next unit expressly addresses those standing servants as sons of Benjamin and questions royal gifts and appointments, identifying the particular audience.

relationship: Royal lands and command appointments recur as patronage language
rationale: Saul asks whether David will give fields, vineyards and command posts; Samuel's earlier royal-claim speech describes commanders and the king giving seized fields and vineyards to servants. The question is not proof that either king has already made every listed grant.

relationship: The accusation of a son-David covenant relates to the recorded oath
rationale: Saul alleges his son's covenant with David is part of a conspiracy; the farewell records Jonathan and David's Lord-witnessed oath between themselves and their seed. It does not independently confirm Saul's claim that Jonathan raised David against him.

relationship: The reporting Doeg matches the earlier Syrian mule-tender notice
rationale: Doeg identifies David's arrival at the priest; the earlier scene already places Doeg the Syrian, tending Saul's mules, at that visit. The repeated designation and office support this internal connection without changing his ethnicity.

relationship: The provisions report corresponds to the narrated bread gift
rationale: Doeg reports provisions along with inquiry and a sword; the earlier narrative expressly has the priest give the presentation loaves. This match concerns the bread, not an assertion that the earlier unit narrates all parts of Doeg's report.

relationship: The reported sword is the specific weapon earlier offered
rationale: Doeg reports the priest giving Goliath's sword; the earlier dialogue offers that named weapon and David requests it, followed by the handover in context. The reported divine inquiry is not added to the earlier sword dialogue.

relationship: Same-chapter the summoned son of Ahitub answers the king's address
rationale: Saul summons Abimelech son of Ahitub and the priestly family; his next address to son of Ahitub receives the answer Here I am. The repeated patronymic identifies the particular respondent within the summoned group.

relationship: Same-chapter the addressed patronymic identifies the summoned priest
rationale: The respondent addressed as son of Ahitub follows the summons of Abimelech son of Ahitub, grounding the dialogue participant in the explicit preceding identity rather than adding another priest's name.

relationship: The conspiracy charge refers to narrated bread and sword assistance
rationale: Saul's charge names bread, sword and inquiry; the earlier visit records the presentation loaves and sword offer with Doeg present. The connection verifies the narrated assistance without endorsing the charge's motive or supplying its unrecorded inquiry scene.

relationship: The son-in-law defense has the earlier narrated marriage as its basis
rationale: The priest calls David the king's son-in-law as part of his defense of David's faithfulness; the earlier account explicitly gives him Michal as wife and calls him the king's son-in-law. The defense's further claims remain the priest's speech.

relationship: Same-chapter the lack-of-knowledge defense answers the conspiracy charge
rationale: Saul charges deliberate conspiracy; the priest asks that no charge be laid against him or his father's house because he knew nothing small or great. His question about beginning inquiry today is not rewritten as a denial that any inquiry ever occurred.

relationship: Same-chapter the death verdict is followed by the stated priest killing
rationale: Saul condemns Abimelech and his father's house; the following execution account gives Doeg's killing of three hundred and five ephoud-wearing men. The later escaped son is not erased by treating the verdict as proof of total extinction.

relationship: Same-chapter the servants' refusal contrasts with Doeg's compliance
rationale: Saul's servants refuse to put their hands against the Lord's priests; after Saul turns the order to Doeg, Doeg strikes them. The contrast preserves the distinct actors and the actual three-hundred-and-five figure.

relationship: Same-chapter doeg performs the priest-killing order the servants refused
rationale: The execution by Doeg follows the explicit refusal of the king's servants to strike the Lord's priests. It does not reassign their refusal to Doeg or replace the supplied ephoud-wearer count.

relationship: Same-chapter the massacre report extends from priests to the priestly city
rationale: The report of three hundred and five priests killed is followed by the named city Nomba and a catalog of residents and livestock struck. The second report expands the described attack beyond the ephoud-wearing group.

relationship: Abiathar's escape and later accompanying role repeat his patronymic
rationale: Abiathar son of Abimelech escapes to David; the later account repeats that father-son identification and flight, adding his descent with David to Keilah carrying an ephoud.

relationship: Same-chapter the report attributes to Saul a killing whose executioner is named earlier
rationale: Abiathar reports that Saul put the Lord's priests to death; the earlier action account names Doeg as the striker and gives three hundred and five. The royal-responsibility report and named executioner are distinguished, while Abiathar's narrated escape remains intact.

relationship: Same-chapter david's hindsight statement concerns Doeg's recorded report
rationale: David says he knew Doeg would tell Saul; the preceding court scene actually records Doeg reporting David's arrival to Saul. The earlier narrator is not made to have already stated David's claimed foreknowledge.

relationship: Same-chapter the escaped priest receives a particular protection offer
rationale: Abiathar flees to David as the explicitly saved son; David offers him a shared place of safety and protection. The offer addresses that flight without asserting all future outcomes for Abiathar.

relationship: Same-chapter the threat at Keilah is answered by the town's narrated rescue
rationale: The report names foreigners attacking Keilah and plundering its threshing floors; the later action defeats those foreigners and explicitly saves Keilah's inhabitants.

relationship: Same-chapter the go-and-save command is followed by the stated rescue
rationale: The Lord tells David to strike the foreigners and save Keilah; David then goes, fights and saves Keilah's inhabitants, matching the particular commanded town and action.

relationship: Same-chapter the men's expressed fear is followed by renewed inquiry
rationale: David's men question going to Keilah while afraid in Judea; David then inquires again and receives another go-down assurance about the foreigners. Their concern and the renewed answer remain distinct voices.

relationship: Same-chapter the repeated inquiry returns to the same proposed intervention
rationale: David inquires again and receives the go-down and foreigners-into-your-hands answer after the initial go-and-save-Keilah response, preserving the two actual formulations.

relationship: Same-chapter the recorded rescue corresponds to the earlier divine direction
rationale: David's company defeats the foreigners and saves the inhabitants, corresponding to the Lord's earlier instruction to strike them and save Keilah. The narrated flight and livestock details are not added to the wording of the command.

relationship: The ephoud-bearing companion is the previously escaped son
rationale: The Keilah notice identifies Abiathar son of Abimelech who fled to David; the earlier escape account supplies that same son and flight. The later ephoud detail is retained without an independent chronology for every movement.

relationship: Same-chapter saul's city-trap inference contrasts with David's actual withdrawal
rationale: Saul says God has sold David into his hands because the city has doors and bars; David's company later leaves Keilah and Saul gives up going out. The claimed divine delivery is not accepted as a narrated capture.

relationship: Same-chapter the proposed siege is abandoned after the company leaves
rationale: Saul orders the people down to hem in David at Keilah; after David leaves and the escape is reported, Saul gives up his going out. No successful siege or capture is inserted.

relationship: Same-chapter the requested ephoud is the object introduced with Abiathar
rationale: David tells Abiathar to bring the Lord's ephoud; the earlier Keilah notice has that same priest arrive with an ephoud in his hand. No unreported consultation mechanism is supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter the prayer's stated threat leads into its actual questions
rationale: David tells the Lord he has heard Saul plans to come against Keilah and destroy it because of him; the following unit asks about closure and Saul's descent. The reply It will be shut up is not rewritten as a different answer.

relationship: Same-chapter the actual oracle is followed by withdrawal from Keilah
rationale: After David's questions and the Lord's actual reply It will be shut up, the next extant unit reports David's company leaving and Saul abandoning his descent. Absent23:12 and an unreported speech about the citizens are not supplied.

relationship: The later company estimate matches the earlier gathering estimate
rationale: About four hundred leave Keilah with David, matching the earlier approximate four hundred who gathered under him. The matching estimates do not independently identify every member of either group.

relationship: Same-chapter the narrator's non-delivery statement contrasts with Saul's delivery claim
rationale: Saul had claimed God sold David into his hands in the city; the later wilderness summary expressly says the Lord did not hand David into Saul's hands. The distinct city and wilderness settings are preserved.

relationship: Same-chapter jonathan comes to the named place where David faces pursuit
rationale: David is at Kaine of Ziph while Saul seeks him; Jonathan then goes to David at Kaine and strengthens him in the Lord, identifying the particular meeting place without modern geography.

relationship: Same-chapter strengthening in the Lord is followed by the actual reassurance
rationale: Jonathan strengthens David's hands in the Lord; his next speech says not to fear, that Saul's hand will not find him and that David will reign. The unit's hand-strengthening phrase is not converted into an independently described physical gesture.

relationship: Jonathan's prospective second place contrasts with Saul's succession argument
rationale: Jonathan says David will reign and he will be second; Saul earlier claimed Jonathan's kingship could not be established while David lived. The differing predictions and arguments are preserved without declaring every future role fulfilled.

relationship: The covenant before the Lord relates to the earlier enduring oath
rationale: The two men make a covenant before the Lord; their earlier farewell oath invokes the Lord's witness between them and their seed for ever, connecting the named bond without reconstructing unstated covenant ceremonies.

relationship: A psalm heading explicitly repeats the Ziphites' report
rationale: The Ziphites tell Saul that David is hidden among them; the supplied Greek-numbered psalm heading repeats those named informants, Saul and that particular question.

relationship: The Ziphite reports repeat the hiding-place accusation
rationale: Both accounts have Ziphites approach Saul and report David among them with the supplied Echela and Jessaimoun descriptions. The parallel reports are not merged into one independently dated event or a modern site identification.

relationship: Same-chapter the invitation and delivery claim receive further reconnaissance instructions
rationale: The informants invite Saul down and claim David is shut into his hands; Saul then tells them to find the place and promises a joint search. Their claim is not independently validated as an accomplished capture.

relationship: Same-chapter saul's blessing responds to the informants' offer of assistance
rationale: Saul blesses the informants for taking trouble for him after their invitation to descend and claim about David. The blessing remains Saul's response rather than a narrator's declaration of divine approval.

relationship: Same-chapter coordinated commands to locate David are repeated and expanded
